# Frequently Asked Questions
Expert answers covering gold rates, karat purities, GST/HST regulations, making charges, and investment insights across Canada.
# Q 1 . How often are gold rates updated in Canada?
Gold rates are compiled from third-party market data and refreshed throughout the trading day when our market feed is available. Every rate table carries a visible Eastern Time timestamp so you know exactly how fresh the numbers are.
# Q 2 . What is the difference between 24K, 22K, 21K, and 18K gold?
24K is pure gold (99.9% purity), making it soft and ideal for bullion bars and coins. 22K contains 91.6% gold, popular for traditional high-carat jewelry. 21K (87.5% purity) and 18K (75.0% purity) contain higher alloy metals for enhanced durability, making them perfect for intricate diamond or gemstone jewelry settings.
# Q 3 . Are making charges included in the spot gold rates shown?

chunks.title: Gold Price FAQs Canada | Rates, Karats & Tax Guide
chunks.text:
No. The prices displayed on our website reflect the intrinsic melt-value of raw gold per gram in Canadian dollars (CAD). Making charges, design complexity fees, and brand premiums are charged separately by Canadian retailers and jewellers, whether you buy from Kitco, Silver Gold Bull, or a local jewellery store.
# Q 4 . Is there any tax on buying gold in Canada?
Investment-grade gold — bars, wafers and coins of 99.5% purity or higher — is GST/HST-exempt across Canada. Jewellery and lower-purity items are taxed at the regular rate: 5% GST in Alberta and the territories, 12% in British Columbia (5% GST + 7% PST), 13% HST in Ontario, and 14.975% in Quebec (5% GST + 9.975% QST).
# Q 5 . Why do gold prices vary slightly between different dealers in Canada?
While the baseline metal rate is anchored to the global spot price converted to Canadian dollars, individual dealers set different premiums depending on fabrication costs, shipping, buy-back spreads, and whether you buy online (e.g., Kitco in Montreal or Silver Gold Bull in Calgary) or from a local jeweller.
# Q 6 . Can visitors claim tax refunds on gold purchases in Canada?

chunks.title: Gold Price FAQs Canada | Rates, Karats & Tax Guide
chunks.text:
No. Unlike some countries, Canada does not operate a tourist tax-refund scheme, so visitors pay the applicable GST/HST or QST on taxable gold purchases (such as jewellery) just like residents. Investment-grade bullion remains tax-exempt for everyone.
# Q 7 . Is it better to buy gold bars (bullion) or jewelry for investment?
For pure investment purposes, 24K gold bars and certified coins — such as Royal Canadian Mint products — are always recommended because they carry minimal fabrication premiums, are GST/HST-exempt, and can be liquidated easily at international spot value with negligible buy-back loss.
# Q 8 . How is the gold price per gram calculated from ounce prices?
Global gold is traded in troy ounces (1 troy ounce = 31.1035 grams). To find the 24K gram price in CAD, we take the international ounce rate converted to Canadian dollars and divide it precisely by 31.1035.
# Q 9 . What factors drive gold price movements in Canada?
Key drivers include US Federal Reserve and Bank of Canada interest rate decisions, the USD/CAD exchange rate (a weaker loonie pushes the CAD gold price up), geopolitical tensions, global inflation, and central bank gold purchases.

Yes, the Canadian gold market is highly liquid. Major bullion dealers such as Kitco, Silver Gold Bull and TD Precious Metals, as well as most local jewellers, will buy back gold items. Carrying your original purchase invoice and keeping Royal Canadian Mint assay certificates or hallmarks intact makes the buy-back faster and smoother.

# Gold Dealers in Canada: Find Reputable Sellers (2026)
The most trusted gold dealers in Canada include Kitco in Montreal, Silver Gold Bull in Calgary, and Border Gold in Vancouver. Whichever dealer you choose, it should pass three checks: years in business, transparent live pricing, and a published buyback policy.
Choosing the right gold dealer is the single most important decision you'll make as a gold buyer — more important than timing the market or picking the perfect product. A reputable dealer gives you fair prices, authentic products, and honest advice. A bad one can cost you thousands through inflated premiums, counterfeit products, or high-pressure sales tactics.
This guide shows you how to find trustworthy gold dealers across Canada, what to verify before handing over your money, and the warning signs that should send you walking.
# Major Gold Dealers by Canadian City
As Canada's financial capital, Toronto has the country's deepest bullion market. The downtown core — particularly around the financial district and the historic jewellery district near Dundas and Yonge — hosts numerous dealers. Competition is fierce, which generally means tighter premiums for buyers.

chunks.title: Gold Dealers in Canada: Find Reputable Sellers (2026)

Established Toronto dealers typically publish live prices on their websites, so you can compare before you visit. Parking and navigating downtown is a hassle, so many Torontonians end up buying online even from local dealers — most offer insured shipping within Ontario.
Vancouver's bullion market serves both local investors and significant demand from the Asia-Pacific community, where gold gifting is a deep tradition. Border Gold, headquartered in Vancouver, is one of Canada's best-known dealers. The city's proximity to Asian markets also means strong demand for 24K jewellery-grade gold alongside investment bullion.
Vancouver buyers should be aware that premiums on certain products (particularly high-purity Asian-style jewellery) can differ from Toronto pricing due to local demand patterns. As always, compare the premium over spot, not just the sticker price.

# 4. BBB Accreditation and Industry Membership

# 5. Clear Buyback Policy

Ask: "If I want to sell this back to you next year, what will you pay?" A trustworthy dealer answers immediately with a formula (e.g., "spot minus 2%"). A dealer that dodges the question, or only sells but never buys, is a red flag.
# 6. Professional Premises and Staff
For walk-in dealers: Is the shop professional? Do staff answer questions knowledgeably without pressuring you? Do they test metals in front of you? Professional dealers welcome scrutiny — they have nothing to hide.
# Red Flags: When to Walk Away
"Rare," "exclusive," or "limited edition" pitches. Classic telemarketer language for massively overpriced coins. Standard bullion is what you want.
Premiums you can't calculate. If the seller can't or won't explain the premium over spot, leave.
Pressure tactics. "This price is only good for the next 10 minutes" has no place in bullion dealing. Gold will still be there tomorrow.
Cash-only, no receipts. Legitimate dealers provide invoices for every transaction. No receipt means no proof of purchase — and no recourse.
Guaranteed returns. Nobody can guarantee gold's future price. Anyone who does is lying.

Unsolicited calls or emails. Reputable bullion dealers don't cold-call. If someone phones you out of the blue to sell gold, hang up.
Prices far below market. Gold at 10% under spot doesn't exist in the legitimate market. It's either counterfeit or a scam.
# Online vs. Local Dealers: Which Is Better?
Choose local when: you're buying for the first time and want to see the product, you're making a large purchase and want to avoid shipping risk, or you value an ongoing relationship with a dealer who knows you.
Choose online when: you want the lowest premiums, the widest selection, or you live far from a major city. Insured shipping in Canada is reliable, and most established dealers ship thousands of orders without incident.
The hybrid approach many experienced buyers use: research and compare online, then buy from whichever reputable dealer — local or online — offers the best all-in price for the specific product you want.
# Questions to Ask Any Dealer Before Buying
1. What is your premium over the live spot price for this product?
2. Is this price in CAD? Are there any additional fees (shipping, insurance, handling)?

3. What is your buyback policy — what would you pay me for this if I sold it back tomorrow?
4. Does this product qualify for the GST/HST exemption?
5. Is the product sealed with assay certification? Can I verify the serial number?
6. How is my shipment insured, and what happens if it's lost?
A good dealer answers all six without hesitation. Their answers should be consistent with what you've read in this guide.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# Who is the most trusted gold dealer in Canada?
There isn't a single "most trusted" dealer — several have excellent decades-long reputations, including Kitco (Montreal), Silver Gold Bull (Calgary), and Border Gold (Vancouver). The right choice depends on your location, what you're buying, and who offers the best premium. Always compare at least two or three.
# Is it safe to buy gold online in Canada?
Yes, when you use established dealers. Look for insured, trackable shipping, discreet packaging, and a dealer with a long track record. Thousands of Canadians buy gold online every week without issues.
# Do gold dealers in Canada report purchases to the government?

No. There is no requirement in Canada to report gold bullion purchases to tax authorities, and dealers don't report your purchases. (Selling at a profit later may have capital gains tax implications — see our selling guide .)
# Can I negotiate with a gold dealer?
On standard bullion products, premiums are usually fixed — but it never hurts to ask, especially on larger orders ($25,000+). Many dealers offer volume discounts or reduced premiums on orders above certain thresholds. On jewellery and estate pieces, negotiation is expected.
# What's the difference between a bullion dealer and a pawn shop?
Bullion dealers specialize in investment-grade precious metals, publish live prices, and deal in certified products. Pawn shops deal in secondhand goods of all kinds and typically pay well below market for gold. For buying investment gold, always use a bullion dealer.
# Should I buy from a US dealer to save money?
Usually not. Any savings on the sticker price are typically erased by currency conversion fees, cross-border shipping, customs brokerage, and the risk of delays. Canadian dealers price in CAD and understand the GST/HST exemption — stick with them.

# Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
You've checked the live gold price, found a dealer, and picked out a beautiful 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf. Then you notice something: the dealer's price is higher than the spot price you saw online. That difference — the premium — is one of the most misunderstood parts of buying gold.
This guide explains exactly what premiums are, why they exist, what Canadians typically pay for different products, and how to keep your premiums as low as possible.
# What Is a Gold Premium?
The spot price is the current market price for one troy ounce of pure gold for immediate delivery — the benchmark number you see on financial news and our live gold price page . It reflects wholesale trading between banks, refiners, and large institutions.
The premium is the amount you pay above spot for a physical product. It's usually expressed as a percentage or a dollar figure per ounce:
Premium = Dealer's selling price − Spot price
Example: If gold spot is CAD $3,400/oz and a dealer sells a 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf for CAD $3,570, the premium is CAD $170, or about 5%.

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
You'll never buy physical gold at exactly spot — and anyone offering it is either selling you something fake or running a scam. Premiums are a normal, legitimate part of the market. The skill is in knowing what's reasonable and what's excessive.
# Why Do Premiums Exist?
Premiums aren't dealer greed — they reflect real costs in the journey from raw gold to the coin or bar in your hand:
# Minting and Manufacturing
Turning a gold bar into a finished coin involves design, die-making, striking, quality control, and anti-counterfeiting features. The Royal Canadian Mint's Gold Maple Leaf, with its radial-line finish and micro-engraved security mark, costs real money to produce. These costs are baked into the premium.
Gold moves from mines → refiners → mints → wholesalers → dealers → you. Each step adds handling, insurance, and transport costs. Coins and bars are high-value, high-security freight — shipping a tube of Gold Maples across Canada fully insured isn't cheap.

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
Dealers are businesses. Their margin covers rent, staff, security systems, inventory financing (gold sitting in a vault ties up capital), and the risk of price movements between buying and selling. Typical dealer gross margins on standard bullion are thinner than most people assume — often just 1–3% on high-volume products.
When demand surges — during financial crises, for example — premiums spike because mints can't increase production instantly. During the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic lockdowns, premiums on popular coins doubled or tripled in Canada as buyers overwhelmed supply. Conversely, in quiet markets, dealers compete and premiums compress.
# Typical Premium Ranges in Canada
These are approximate ranges for established Canadian dealers in normal market conditions. Actual premiums move with market conditions, order size, and the specific dealer.
# Government Bullion Coins (1 oz)
Gold Maple Leaf (1 oz): 4–6% over spot
American Gold Eagle (1 oz): 5–7% over spot
Krugerrand (1 oz): 4–6% over spot
The Maple Leaf typically carries the lowest premium in Canada — it's the home-team coin, and domestic supply chains are shortest.

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
# Fractional Coins (1/2 oz, 1/4 oz, 1/10 oz)
Expect 8–15% over spot , sometimes higher for 1/10 oz pieces. Smaller coins cost nearly as much to manufacture as full-ounce coins, so the per-ounce premium is much higher. Fractional coins make sense for divisibility and gifting, not for minimizing cost per ounce.
1 oz bars: 3–5% over spot
10 oz bars: 2.5–4% over spot
1 kg bars: 2–3.5% over spot
1 gram bars: 15–30% over spot (avoid for investment — the premium is brutal)
Bars from recognized refiners (PAMP Suisse, Valcambi, Royal Canadian Mint, Johnson Matthey) command slightly higher premiums than generic bars but are far easier to resell.
# 99.99% vs. 99.5% Products
Higher-purity products from prestigious mints carry modestly higher premiums than basic .999 bars — usually less than 1% extra. The liquidity and GST/HST advantages are worth it for most Canadian buyers.
Jewellery premiums are in a different universe: 100–400% over melt value is normal at retail. You're paying for design, craftsmanship, brand, and retail overhead — not gold content. This is why jewellery is for wearing, not investing.
# Factors That Affect Your Premium

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
As shown above, the single biggest factor. A 1 kg bar and a 1/10 oz coin contain gold worth the same per ounce at spot — but you'll pay wildly different premiums.
Dealers reward volume. Buying 10 ounces at once typically earns a lower per-ounce premium than buying one ounce. Many Canadian dealers publish tiered pricing: the premium drops at 10 oz, 50 oz, and 100 oz thresholds. If you're planning to accumulate over time, consider saving up for fewer, larger purchases.
Bank wire or Interac e-Transfer usually gets you the best price. Credit card payments add 2–3% (the dealer's processing cost, passed to you). Some dealers also charge extra for PayPal. Always ask about payment-method pricing.
In calm markets, dealers keep inventory lean and premiums tight. When prices swing violently, dealers widen premiums to protect against losses between purchase and sale. If premiums seem unusually high across all dealers simultaneously, it's the market — not any individual dealer gouging.
# The CAD Exchange Rate

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
Gold is priced globally in USD. When the Canadian dollar weakens, the CAD spot price rises even if the USD price is flat — and some dealers' premiums effectively widen during currency volatility. There's nothing you can do about this except be aware of it.
# How to Minimize Premiums: 8 Proven Strategies
The per-ounce premium on a 10 oz bar is roughly half that of ten 1 oz coins. If your budget allows, size up.
# 2. Stick to Standard Products
The 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf is the lowest-premium coin available to Canadians. Exotic coins, "limited editions," and commemorative issues carry higher premiums you'll never recover on resale.
# 3. Compare the Premium, Not the Price
Dealer A sells a Maple at $3,570 when spot is $3,400 (5% premium). Dealer B sells at $3,555 when spot is $3,380 (5.2% premium). Dealer A's headline price is higher, but their premium is lower — and premiums are what you actually control. Always do the math.
# 4. Pay by Wire or E-Transfer
Avoid credit card surcharges. The 2–3% you save goes straight to your bottom line.
# 5. Buy During Quiet Markets

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
Premiums compress when demand is low — typically during summer doldrums or extended sideways markets. Nobody can time the gold price reliably, but you can avoid buying during panic-driven premium spikes.
# 6. Consider Secondary Market (Pre-Owned) Bullion
Many dealers sell "secondary market" or "circulated" coins and bars — authentic products bought back from customers, sold at 1–2% lower premiums than brand-new items. The gold is identical; only the packaging is less pristine. This is one of the best-kept secrets for premium-conscious buyers.
# 7. Build a Dealer Relationship
Repeat customers often get better pricing, early access to deals, and honest advice. Loyalty pays in this business.
# 8. Watch for Dealer Specials
Canadian dealers regularly run promotions — reduced premiums on specific products, free shipping thresholds, or volume discounts. Sign up for a couple of dealers' email lists (just the reputable ones) to catch these.
# Premiums When Selling: The Other Side
Premiums work in reverse when you sell. Dealers buy back gold below spot — typically 1–3% under for standard bullion. This buy-sell spread is how dealers stay in business.

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
The round-trip cost of buying and selling is the buy premium plus the sell discount. Example:
Buy 1 oz Maple at 5% over spot
Sell later at 2% under spot
Total round-trip cost: ~7% of the gold's value
This means gold needs to appreciate roughly 7% for you to break even on a quick flip — one reason gold rewards patient, long-term holders rather than traders.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# What is a good premium for a Gold Maple Leaf in Canada?
In normal market conditions, 4–6% over spot for a 1 oz coin is fair. Below 4% is excellent (often volume pricing or secondary market). Above 7% in calm markets means you should shop around.
# Why are premiums higher for smaller gold coins?
Manufacturing costs don't scale down with size — striking a 1/10 oz coin costs nearly as much as striking a 1 oz coin. The fixed production cost is spread over less gold, so the per-ounce premium is higher.
# Do premiums change daily?
The premium percentage is relatively stable day to day, but the dollar amount moves with the spot price. During major news events or market stress, premium percentages themselves can spike — sometimes dramatically.
# Are online premiums lower than in-store?

chunks.title: Gold Premiums Explained: What Canadians Pay Over Spot
chunks.text:
Generally yes, by 0.5–2%. Online dealers have lower overhead. However, factor in shipping costs on small orders — a $30 shipping fee on a single 1/10 oz coin can erase the online advantage.
# Should I wait for lower premiums before buying?
Don't try to time premiums precisely — it's as hard as timing the gold price. But do avoid buying during obvious panic spikes (when every headline screams crisis, premiums are usually at their worst). Patient buyers who purchase during calm periods consistently pay less.
# Do I pay premium on top of GST/HST?
Investment-grade bullion (99.5%+ pure) is GST/HST exempt in Canada, so you pay only the premium over spot. On jewellery and non-qualifying products, tax applies on top of the already-high retail markup.

# Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
On the morning of October 10, 2026, Canadians woke up to two headlines at once: the economy had just shed 68,300 jobs, and the Canadian dollar was tumbling toward its weakest level against the US dollar since April 2025. Within hours, gold briefly punched above US$4,200 an ounce for the first time that week. In Canadian dollars, the metal was sitting around C$5,845 an ounce — near the top of its recent range.
If you buy or sell gold in Canada, this combination — bad jobs news, a sinking loonie, and a stubbornly high gold price — is not a coincidence. It is a textbook example of how Canadian gold prices are actually set. This article walks through the chain, one link at a time: the September jobs report, the currency reaction, and the simple arithmetic that turns a US-dollar gold price into the number you see on a dealer's price board in Toronto, Calgary, or Montreal.
# The September jobs report: worse than anyone expected

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
Statistics Canada released its September Labour Force Survey on Friday, October 9, and the numbers were grim across the board. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a modest gain of roughly 9,200 jobs. Instead, employers cut a net 68,300 jobs — the second straight monthly decline after a loss of about 41,700 in August.
Employment change: −68,300 (−0.3%)
Unemployment rate: 6.5%, up from 6.4% in August
Full-time employment: −35,400; part-time: −32,900
Labour-force participation: 64.8%, the lowest since December 1997 outside the pandemic years
Young workers (15–24): −48,000 jobs, their unemployment near 13%
Public sector: −70,000 employees, the fourth straight monthly decline
Quebec lost 49,000 jobs and British Columbia 20,000, while Alberta added 23,000. Net job losses for 2026 stood at about 41,200 for the year to date — a sharp contrast with the gain of over 211,000 recorded in the same stretch a year earlier.

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
For gold markets, the jobs report mattered for one reason above all: it forced a repricing of what the Bank of Canada might do next. With growth sagging and tariffs biting, expectations for a rate hold or cut at the October 28 policy decision shifted — and that repricing hit the currency immediately.
# The loonie's slide: toward 1.43
Currency markets reacted within minutes of the release. The USD/CAD pair jumped to 1.42987 at 12:35 UTC on October 10 — levels against the US dollar last seen in April 2025, and just short of the 1.43 line that analysts at Rabobank had flagged as the next threshold. It closed the day at 1.42566, up 0.22%.
Why did the currency fall so hard? A few forces are stacking up against the loonie:
Rate expectations. Weaker labour data raises the odds that the Bank of Canada pauses or eases at its October 28 decision, narrowing the rate advantage — or widening the rate gap — against the US dollar.
Tariff drag. US Section 338 tariffs of 50% on hundreds of Canadian goods lines (plus sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber) are weighing on the growth outlook. A currency is, in the end, a claim on future growth — and markets are repricing Canada's.

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
Safe-haven flows. When uncertainty rises, global capital gravitates toward the US dollar. The same fear trade that lifts gold in US dollars tends to depress the loonie.
The result is a familiar pattern for Canadians: the currency that defines their paycheques and prices is weakening at exactly the moment a crisis hedge is rallying.
# Why a weak loonie pushes gold higher in Canada: the arithmetic
Here is the part that surprises many first-time buyers: gold is priced worldwide in US dollars, and the Canadian price is simply the US price multiplied by the exchange rate.
CAD gold price = USD spot price × USD/CAD rate
Take October 19, 2026, as an example. Spot gold was around US$4,145 an ounce, and the loonie was trading near 1.41 to the dollar:
US$4,145 × 1.41 ≈ C$5,845 per ounce
Now imagine the same US$4,145 price with a stronger loonie at 1.32: US$4,145 × 1.32 ≈ C$5,471 per ounce — a difference of nearly C$375 on the same global gold price. This is why gold in Canada can rise even on days when the US-dollar price falls: if the loonie weakens faster than gold slips, the Canadian price climbs anyway.

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
Conversely, it means Canadian buyers should never judge a deal by the US price alone. What matters for your wallet is the C$-denominated number, and that number is hostage to two moving parts, not one.
# Where CAD gold stands now: near recent highs, not the all-time record
Let's be precise, because precision matters when money is involved. As of October 19, 2026, gold in Canadian dollars was trading around C$5,845 an ounce and C$188 per gram for 24K — near the upper end of its range for recent weeks.
But this is not the all-time record. The highest price of gold in Canada over the last ten years was about C$7,345 per ounce on January 28, 2026 , when the global price hit its record near US$5,597. Since then, the US-dollar price has fallen roughly 25%, and the weak loonie has only partially offset that decline for Canadians. A year ago, on October 19, 2025, gold was around C$5,962 — so Canadians are actually paying slightly less in loonie terms than a year earlier, even though the currency has weakened.

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
The honest way to describe today's market: CAD gold is holding near its recent highs despite a falling US-dollar price , and the weak loonie is the only reason it hasn't fallen further. If you are a seller, your gold still commands a historically elevated price. If you are a buyer, you are paying a currency surcharge on top of the metal.
# What record-adjacent prices mean for buyers and sellers
For buyers. A high CAD price means the loonie is quietly taxing every purchase. The practical response is to focus on what you can control: the premium over spot you pay your dealer, not the spot number itself. On a 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf, dealer premiums typically run 2–7% over spot; banks tend to charge more. See our guide on where to buy gold in Canada: banks vs dealers for a direct price comparison.
For sellers. A historically elevated CAD price is your friend. Jewellery, scrap gold, and coins you bought years ago are worth dramatically more in nominal loonie terms. Shop your buyback quotes the same way you would a purchase: get at least three, and compare the payout as a percentage of spot.

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
For everyone. Remember that investment-grade bullion (99.5% pure or higher) is exempt from GST/HST across Canada. High prices do not change that — the exemption applies to the purity, not the price level.
# Outlook: what could move CAD gold next
Three catalysts are on the calendar:
Bank of Canada, October 28. More weak data could cement expectations of easier policy, pressuring the loonie further — supportive for CAD gold even if the USD price drifts.
US tariffs. Section 338 levies and sectoral tariffs continue to hang over Canadian exports; any escalation would likely weaken the loonie again.
The US rate path. The Fed meets October 27–28, the same week. Fading hike expectations have supported gold; a surprise either way moves the USD leg of the equation.
There is also a longer-term undercurrent: with gold roughly 25% below its January record in US dollars, any renewed safe-haven bid would hit the CAD price with a multiplier, because a weaker loonie amplifies every US-dollar rally.
# Frequently asked questions
# Why is gold more expensive in Canada than the US price suggests?

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
Because the Canadian price equals the US-dollar spot price multiplied by the USD/CAD exchange rate. When the loonie weakens (a higher USD/CAD number), each US dollar of gold costs more Canadian dollars — even if the global price hasn't moved.
# Did the September jobs report cause gold to rise in Canada?
Indirectly, yes. The loss of 68,300 jobs (far worse than the expected 9,200 gain) pushed down the loonie by raising expectations of easier Bank of Canada policy. Since CAD gold = USD price × exchange rate, the weaker currency lifted the Canadian price — and gold simultaneously topped US$4,200 on safe-haven demand.
# Is gold at an all-time high in Canada right now?
No. As of October 19, 2026, gold was around C$5,845 an ounce — near recent highs but roughly 20% below the all-time record of about C$7,345 set on January 28, 2026. The weak loonie is cushioning the fall from January's peak rather than setting a new one.
# Should I buy gold now or wait for the loonie to recover?

chunks.title: Gold Near Highs in Canada: Weak Loonie Holding Prices Up
chunks.text:
No one can time either market reliably. A practical approach: if you are buying for the long term, focus on minimizing the premium over spot (compare at least three dealers), because the premium is the one cost fully under your control. If you are waiting for a stronger loonie, be aware it could take months — and a stronger loonie often arrives alongside a stronger US economy, which can push the USD gold price up at the same time.
# Does the exchange rate affect selling gold too?
Yes, in the same direction. A weak loonie raises the Canadian-dollar value of the gold you already own. Sellers get the mirror image of buyers' pain: historically elevated CAD prices make it a reasonable time to take profits on pieces you no longer want.
# How can I convert the US gold price to Canadian dollars myself?
Multiply the US-dollar spot price by the current USD/CAD rate. Example: US$4,145 × 1.41 = C$5,845 per ounce. Divide by 31.1035 for the per-gram price (about C$188/g at 24K). Our gold calculator does this automatically with live rates.

# How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
The easiest way to buy gold in Canada is through an established bullion dealer — in person or online — choosing investment-grade products of 99.5% purity or higher, such as the 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf, which are exempt from GST/HST.
Buying gold in Canada has never been easier — or more popular. Whether you want to protect your savings from inflation, diversify your portfolio, or simply own a tangible asset, gold remains one of the most trusted stores of value in Canadian history. But buying gold for the first time raises plenty of questions: Where do you buy it? How much over the spot price should you pay? Do you owe tax? Where do you keep it?
This guide answers all of that. By the end, you'll know exactly how to buy gold in Canada with confidence.
# Where to Buy Gold in Canada
Canadians have four main options for buying physical gold. Each has its strengths, and the best choice depends on how much you're buying and how comfortable you are with the process.
# Local Gold and Bullion Dealers

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
Every major Canadian city has established bullion dealers with physical storefronts. These shops buy and sell gold coins, bars, and sometimes jewellery. The big advantage of buying locally is that you can inspect the product before you pay, walk out with gold in hand the same day, and build a relationship with a dealer you trust.
Well-known Canadian dealers include Kitco in Montreal, Silver Gold Bull in Calgary, Border Gold in Vancouver, and several reputable shops in Toronto's financial district and jewellery district. When choosing a local dealer, look for one that has been in business for many years, displays buy and sell prices openly, and is willing to answer your questions patiently.
# Online Bullion Dealers
Buying gold online is the most popular option for many Canadians today. Online dealers typically offer lower premiums than walk-in shops because their overhead is lower, and they carry a wider selection. Most ship fully insured via Canada Post or private courier, with discreet packaging.

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
Reputable Canadian online dealers include Silver Gold Bull, Kitco, Border Gold, and Colonial Acres Coins. When ordering online, confirm that prices are quoted in Canadian dollars (CAD), check the shipping and insurance policy, and read the buyback policy — a dealer that also buys back gold is a good sign.
One caution: stick to dealers based in Canada or with a strong Canadian presence. Ordering from US dealers can trigger customs delays, brokerage fees, and currency conversion costs that wipe out any savings.
Canada's big banks — including TD, RBC, and Scotiabank (through ScotiaMocatta, its precious metals division) — sell gold bars and coins to customers. Bank-sold gold is as trustworthy as it gets, and some banks offer allocated storage. The downside is that bank premiums tend to be higher than dealer premiums, and selection is usually limited to standard bars and coins.
Banks are a solid option if you value maximum peace of mind and don't mind paying a bit more.
# The Royal Canadian Mint

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
The Royal Canadian Mint, based in Ottawa, produces the world-famous Gold Maple Leaf coin — one of the most recognized and liquid gold coins on the planet, struck in 99.99% pure gold. You can buy directly from the Mint's website or through authorized dealers. Mint-direct purchases sometimes carry higher premiums, but you're getting product straight from the source.
# What to Look for When Buying Gold
For investment purposes, buy gold that is at least 99.5% pure (often marked .999 or .9999 fine). This matters for two reasons: purer gold is easier to resell at full value, and in Canada, investment-grade gold of 99.5%+ purity is exempt from GST/HST. Lower-purity gold — like 14K jewellery — is harder to value precisely and doesn't qualify for the tax exemption.
# Weight and Denomination
Gold bars come in sizes from 1 gram up to 1 kilogram (and larger). Coins typically come in 1 oz, 1/2 oz, 1/4 oz, and 1/10 oz sizes. Smaller denominations cost more per gram (higher premiums) but are easier to sell in portions later. A common strategy for beginners: start with a 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf or a 10 oz bar, then add smaller pieces over time.

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
The "spot price" is the live market price of one troy ounce of pure gold. You'll never buy physical gold at exactly spot — dealers add a premium to cover minting, distribution, and their margin. Understanding premiums is essential, so read our dedicated guide to gold premiums in Canada .
Buy products from recognized mints (Royal Canadian Mint, Perth Mint, US Mint, PAMP Suisse, Valcambi) that come sealed in assay packaging with a serial number and certificate. Avoid deals that seem too good to be true, unmarked bars, and sellers who can't explain what they're selling.
# GST/HST on Gold in Canada: The Good News
Here's something many first-time buyers don't know: investment-grade gold is exempt from GST/HST in Canada. Under federal tax rules, gold bars, ingots, and coins of at least 99.5% purity are treated as financial instruments rather than goods, so no GST or HST is charged.
This is a significant saving — 5% GST (or up to 15% HST in some provinces) on a $3,000+ purchase adds up fast. Just remember:
The exemption applies to bullion (bars, wafers, and qualifying coins), not jewellery.
Gold jewellery, decorative items, and numismatic/collectible coins are subject to GST/HST.

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
Always confirm with your dealer that the product qualifies before assuming the exemption.
If a dealer tries to charge you GST/HST on a 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf, something is wrong — walk away and buy elsewhere.
# Storage Options for Your Gold
Once you own gold, you need somewhere safe to keep it. Your options:
A high-quality home safe (bolted to the floor, fire-rated) works for modest holdings. It's free and gives you instant access. The risks are obvious: theft, fire, and the fact that most home insurance policies cap valuables coverage — often at just $1,000–$5,000 for bullion unless you buy a separate rider. If you store gold at home, tell as few people as possible and consider a proper safe, not a drawer.
# Bank Safety Deposit Box
Safety deposit boxes at Canadian banks cost roughly $60–$300 per year depending on size. They're far more secure than a home safe and inexpensive. Downsides: limited access hours, and contents are not insured by the bank or CDIC — you'd need separate insurance.
# Third-Party Vault Storage

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
Companies like Brink's and other private vaults offer allocated storage: your specific bars and coins are stored under your name, fully insured, and independently audited. This is the professional choice for larger holdings (typically $25,000+). Fees usually run 0.5%–1% of holdings per year. Some dealers offer storage programs directly.
# Unallocated vs. Allocated
If a dealer or bank offers "gold storage," ask whether it's allocated (specific bars with serial numbers held in your name — you own them outright) or unallocated (a claim on a pool of gold — you're a creditor). Allocated is safer; unallocated is cheaper but carries counterparty risk.
# Tips for First-Time Gold Buyers in Canada
1. Start small. Buy a single 1 oz coin before committing larger sums. Get comfortable with the process.
2. Compare premiums, not just prices. Two dealers selling the same coin at different prices are really offering different premiums — always calculate the premium over the live spot price.
3. Check the buyback policy. A dealer who publishes live buy prices will almost certainly treat you fairly when you sell.

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
4. Keep your receipts and certificates. They prove authenticity and purchase price, which matters for resale and taxes.
5. Beware of "rare coin" pitches. Telemarketers selling overpriced "collectible" or "exclusive" coins are a classic scam. Stick to standard bullion.
6. Dollar-cost average. Instead of trying to time the market, buy a fixed dollar amount regularly — monthly or quarterly.
7. Understand the CAD factor. Gold is priced globally in USD, but you buy in CAD. A rising Canadian dollar makes gold cheaper for you; a falling loonie makes it more expensive — independent of the gold price itself.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# Is it legal to buy gold in Canada?
Yes, completely. There are no restrictions on private gold ownership in Canada, no reporting requirements for purchases, and no limits on how much you can own.
# What is the best gold to buy in Canada?
For most Canadians, the 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf is the best all-round choice: 99.99% pure, GST/HST exempt, instantly recognizable, and easy to resell anywhere in the world. For larger purchases, 10 oz or 1 kg bars from recognized refiners offer lower premiums per ounce.
# How much gold should a beginner buy?

chunks.title: How to Buy Gold in Canada: The Complete 2026 Guide
chunks.text:
There's no magic number, but financial advisors who recommend gold typically suggest 5–10% of a portfolio in precious metals. Start with what you're comfortable with — even a single gram bar or a 1/10 oz coin gets you started.
# Do I pay tax when I buy gold in Canada?
Not on investment-grade bullion (99.5%+ pure) — it's GST/HST exempt. You may owe capital gains tax later when you sell at a profit (see our guide to selling gold in Canada ).
# Can I buy gold with my RRSP or TFSA?
Yes. Certain gold products — including Gold Maple Leafs and bars from accredited refiners — are qualified investments for registered accounts. Many Canadians hold gold through a self-directed RRSP using a precious-metals dealer that offers registered-account services. Rules are specific, so confirm eligibility before buying.
# What's the difference between buying gold in CAD vs. USD?
The product is identical; only the currency differs. Canadian dealers quote in CAD based on the USD spot price converted at the current exchange rate. Always compare the premium over spot rather than the headline price when shopping across borders.

# Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
Whether you're cashing in on years of appreciation, liquidating an inherited collection, or simply rebalancing your portfolio, selling gold in Canada is straightforward — if you know how the market works. The difference between selling smart and selling hastily can easily be 10–20% of your gold's value.
This guide covers where to sell, how pricing works, what paperwork you need, the tax implications, and how to squeeze every dollar out of your sale.
# Where to Sell Gold in Canada
# Local Bullion Dealers
For investment-grade bullion (coins, bars), your best option is usually the same type of dealer you bought from. Established bullion dealers publish live buy prices and pay the closest to market value — typically 1–3% below spot for standard products like Gold Maple Leafs.
Call ahead or check the dealer's website for their current buy prices. Bring your gold in, they'll verify authenticity (usually with electronic testing, in front of you), and you'll walk out with payment the same day — usually by bank draft, e-transfer, or cheque for larger amounts.

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
Several Canadian dealers buy by mail: you request an insured shipping kit, send your gold, they assess it, and pay you after you accept their offer. This works well if you don't live near a dealer. The reputable names are the same ones that sell bullion — be wary of mail-in buyers you've never heard of.
Important: Never send gold to a buyer before agreeing on the valuation method. Legitimate mail-in buyers insure your shipment both ways and give you the right to decline their offer and have your gold returned.
For scrap gold, dental gold, or large quantities of mixed-karat jewellery, selling directly to a refiner can get you the best price — refiners pay based on actual gold content with minimal margin. However, most refiners have minimum lot sizes (often 1–2 ounces of pure gold content) and pay by assay after melting, which takes days. This route suits estate liquidations and jewellers, not someone selling a single chain.
Pawn shops will buy your gold — but expect 30–50% below its actual value. They serve people who need cash immediately and have no other options. If you have any alternative, use it. The convenience premium pawn shops charge is enormous.

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
Selling directly to another individual (through classified ads or collector forums) can sometimes beat dealer prices, since there's no middleman. But it comes with real risks: counterfeit payment, personal safety when meeting strangers with valuables, and no recourse if something goes wrong. If you go this route, meet at a bank, accept only verified payment (bank draft verified with the issuing bank), and never ship before payment clears.
Some Canadian banks buy back gold products they sold, but policies vary and spreads can be wide. Worth asking if you originally bought from a bank, but rarely the best price.
# How Gold Selling Prices Work
# The Buy Price vs. Spot
Dealers quote a buy price (also called the bid) — what they'll pay you — which sits below the spot price. The gap covers their costs and profit margin. For standard bullion in Canada:
1 oz Gold Maple Leaf: typically spot minus 1–2%
Recognized bars (PAMP, Valcambi, RCM): spot minus 1–3%
Generic or unrecognized bars: spot minus 3–5%
Gold jewellery (14K, 18K): 60–80% of melt value
Scrap/dental gold: 70–85% of melt value (after refining costs)
# Melt Value: The Floor Price

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
Melt value is what your gold is worth purely as metal — weight × purity × spot price. It's the absolute floor for any legitimate transaction. Calculate it before you sell anything:
Melt value = (weight in grams ÷ 31.1035) × purity × spot price per troy ounce
For example, a 10-gram 18K chain (75% pure) with gold at CAD $3,400/oz:
(10 ÷ 31.1035) × 0.75 × $3,400 = ~$820 melt value
Our gold calculator does this math for you instantly.
# Why Jewellery Sells Below Melt
That 18K chain has $820 of gold in it, but a dealer might offer you $600–$650. Why? The dealer must refine it (melt it down, separate the alloys, recast) — a process with real costs. Plus they take price risk holding it, and they need a profit margin. Expect 60–80% of melt for jewellery; anyone offering 90%+ is either a refiner or being generous.
Bullion is different: a sealed 1 oz Maple Leaf needs no refining, so it trades within a couple percent of spot.
# What You Need to Sell Gold in Canada

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
All reputable Canadian gold buyers require valid government-issued photo ID (driver's licence or passport) for every transaction. This isn't the dealer being difficult — it's the law. Federal anti-money-laundering regulations and provincial secondhand-dealer laws require buyers to record seller identity.
# Proof of Ownership (Helpful, Not Always Required)
For bullion in original packaging, receipts aren't usually necessary — the product speaks for itself. For estate gold or large quantities, having purchase receipts, inheritance documents, or an estate executor's letter smooths the process and can help with tax reporting later.
Expect the dealer to photocopy your ID and record the items purchased, weights, and prices. This is standard and legally required. If a buyer offers to skip the paperwork for a "better cash price," walk away — they're either evading taxes or fencing stolen goods, and you don't want to be involved.
# No Reporting Threshold to Worry About (for You)

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
Unlike the US (which has certain IRS reporting thresholds for specific bullion sales), Canada has no transaction reporting threshold that triggers automatic tax authority notification on gold sales. You simply report any capital gains on your tax return (see below).
# Tax Implications: Capital Gains on Gold in Canada
# Is Gold Taxable When You Sell?
It depends on what you sell and at what profit:
Investment bullion (bars, Maple Leafs, wafers) is generally treated as capital property — or in some cases as a commodity investment. If you sell at a profit, the gain is a capital gain , and a portion of it is included in your taxable income for the year. Capital losses can offset capital gains.
Personal jewellery worn and enjoyed for years is typically considered personal-use property . Canada's tax rules exempt the first $1,000 of proceeds on personal-use property — and more importantly, if you sell personal jewellery at a loss (which is common, given retail markups), that loss is deemed to be zero and can't be claimed. Gains on personal-use property above the threshold are technically taxable, though in practice the CRA rarely pursues small personal jewellery sales.

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
For investment gold, keep:
Purchase receipts (date, price, product, dealer)
Any storage or insurance costs (these add to your adjusted cost base)
Without purchase records, the CRA can treat your entire sale proceeds as gain. That shoebox of receipts is worth real money.
If your gold is held inside a registered account (self-directed RRSP holding eligible bullion), sales within the account trigger no immediate tax — normal registered-account rules apply (tax on RRSP withdrawal, tax-free TFSA withdrawal).
Disclaimer: Tax rules are complex and change. This is general information, not tax advice. For significant sales, consult a Canadian tax professional — the fee is trivial compared to getting it wrong.
# How to Get the Best Price: 10 Tips
1. Know your melt value first. Calculate it before talking to any buyer. Knowledge is leverage.
2. Get three quotes minimum. Prices vary enormously — especially for jewellery and scrap. Three quotes take an hour and can mean hundreds of dollars.
3. Separate your items. Don't sell bullion and jewellery as one lot. Bullion commands near-spot; jewellery doesn't. Selling them together means everything gets jewellery pricing.

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
4. Don't clean or polish aggressively. Harsh cleaning can remove gold (especially on plated items) and won't increase offers. A gentle wipe is fine.
5. Remove non-gold parts. Take out watch movements, gemstones, and non-gold clasps before weighing — or at least know they're there. Some buyers deduct for them; others let you keep stones.
6. Sell bullion as bullion. Keep coins in original capsules and bars in assay packaging. Breaking the seal can reduce the price.
7. Time your sale. You can't perfectly time markets, but selling during a price spike obviously beats selling in a dip. Check the live gold price trend before deciding.
8. Avoid "cash for gold" mall kiosks. Their business model depends on paying far below market. They're convenient the way a payday lender is convenient.
9. Negotiate. Buy prices aren't always fixed, especially for larger lots. "Can you do a bit better?" costs nothing to ask.
10. Consider partial sales. If gold has risen and you want to take some profit, sell a portion and keep the rest. You don't have to go all-or-nothing.

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
Inherited gold often comes with no documentation and mixed items. Sort bullion from jewellery, get each appraised separately, and document fair market value at inheritance with a dated appraisal — that's your cost base for tax purposes.
Large quantities ($50,000+): get competitive bids from 2–3 major dealers, consider selling in tranches, and ask about wire transfer for payment.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# Where can I sell a Gold Maple Leaf in Canada?
Any established bullion dealer — Kitco, Silver Gold Bull, Border Gold, or your local coin shop. Expect 98–99% of spot for a 1 oz coin in good condition. Call ahead for the day's buy price.
# How much will a pawn shop give me for gold?
Typically 30–50% of melt value — far below a bullion dealer. Only as an absolute last resort.
# Do I need a receipt to sell gold?
Not usually for standard bullion — dealers verify the product itself. Receipts help for large or unusual items and are essential for accurate tax reporting. No legitimate dealer buys without recording your ID, receipt or not.
# Is there a limit on how much gold I can sell in Canada?

chunks.title: Selling Gold in Canada: Where to Sell & What You'll Get
chunks.text:
No legal limit. You can sell any quantity. Very large transactions may prompt standard anti-money-laundering questions from the dealer, which is normal.
# How quickly will I get paid?
Bullion dealers typically pay same-day for standard products — often within the hour. Mail-in services take 3–7 business days including shipping and assessment. Refiners paying on assay results may take 1–2 weeks.
# Should I sell my gold jewellery to a jeweller or a gold buyer?
A gold buyer pays for metal content — best for plain pieces. A jeweller or estate buyer might pay more for designer or antique pieces where craftsmanship has residual value. Get quotes from both for anything beyond scrap.
# What happens if my gold is counterfeit?

# Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
Walk into any Canadian gold shop and you'll see numbers everywhere: 24K, 22K, 18K, 14K, .999, .9999, 585, 750. For newcomers, it's alphabet soup. But understanding gold purity is essential — it determines what your gold is actually worth, whether it's GST/HST exempt, and how easily you can resell it.
This guide breaks down the karat system, explains what each purity level means in practice, and shows you how Canadian standards protect buyers.
# The Karat System Explained
"Karat" (abbreviated K or kt) measures gold purity on a scale of 24. Pure gold is 24 karat. The karat number tells you how many parts out of 24 are pure gold:
24K = 24/24 = 100% pure gold (in practice, 99.9%+)
18K = 18/24 = 75% pure gold
14K = 14/24 = 58.3% pure gold
10K = 10/24 = 41.7% pure gold (the legal minimum to be called "gold" in Canada and the US)
The remaining percentage is made up of alloy metals — silver, copper, nickel, zinc, or palladium — added to make gold harder and more durable, and to alter its colour. Pure 24K gold is relatively soft; you can scratch it with a fingernail. That's why jewellery is rarely 24K.
# Decimal and Millesimal Fineness

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
You'll also see purity expressed as a decimal: .999 means 99.9% pure, .9999 means 99.99% pure. Jewellery often uses a three-digit millesimal stamp: 750 = 18K, 585 = 14K, 417 = 10K. These are just different ways of saying the same thing.
# 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K: What Each Means for You
# 24K Gold (99.9%+ Pure)
The purest form commonly available. In Canada, 24K means investment-grade bullion: Gold Maple Leafs (.9999 fine), kilobars, and wafers from accredited refiners. This is the gold that qualifies for the GST/HST exemption and trades closest to the spot price.
24K is too soft for everyday jewellery, though it's popular for ceremonial and high-end pieces in some cultures. If your goal is wealth preservation or investment, 24K bullion is the standard.
# 22K Gold (91.6% Pure)
Common in 22K jewellery — especially South Asian, Middle Eastern, and East Asian styles widely sold in Vancouver, Toronto, and Surrey. Many classic gold coins are also 22K, including the South African Krugerrand and the American Gold Eagle. These coins contain a full troy ounce of pure gold, but weigh slightly more than an ounce because of the alloy.

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
22K jewellery is a cultural staple for many Canadian families, but note: as jewellery, it's subject to GST/HST, and resale typically happens at a discount to melt value.
The sweet spot for fine jewellery in Canada and Europe. Hard enough for daily wear, rich enough in gold content to hold significant intrinsic value. Most high-end Canadian jewellery — engagement rings, luxury watches, designer pieces — is 18K. Stamped "750" in the millesimal system.
# 14K Gold (58.3% Pure)
The most common jewellery gold in North America. Durable, affordable, and available everywhere. Most mass-market rings, chains, and bracelets sold in Canadian malls are 14K. It holds meaningful gold value but contains less than three-fifths pure gold — something to remember when selling.
# 10K Gold (41.7% Pure)
The minimum purity that can legally be marketed as gold jewellery in Canada. Common in inexpensive pieces. From an investment standpoint, 10K gold is barely worth considering — you're mostly paying for craftsmanship and retail markup.
# Hallmarks: How to Read Gold Stamps

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
Canadian law requires that gold items carrying a quality mark (like "18K") meet strict standards. Here's how to read the stamps you'll encounter:
24K / 999 / 9999 — Investment-grade pure gold
22K / 916 — 91.6% pure (common in coins and cultural jewellery)
18K / 750 — 75% pure (fine jewellery standard)
14K / 585 — 58.3% pure (common North American jewellery)
10K / 417 — 41.7% pure (minimum for "gold" labelling)
GP / EP / RGP — Gold plated, electroplated, or rolled gold plate. These contain only a microscopic layer of gold over base metal. Not solid gold — worth very little as metal.
Maker's marks — Reputable manufacturers stamp their trademark alongside the purity mark.
Canadian legal note: Under the Precious Metals Marking Act, it's illegal in Canada to mark an item with a gold quality mark unless it genuinely meets that standard (within tight tolerances). Mis-marking is a federal offence. This law is a genuine consumer protection — but it only helps if you buy from legitimate sellers.
# Canadian Standards and the GST/HST Threshold

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
The magic number in Canadian gold investing is 99.5% purity . Gold bars, ingots, wafers, and coins meeting or exceeding this threshold are classified as investment-grade precious metals and are exempt from GST/HST nationwide.
This is why Canadian investors overwhelmingly buy .999 or .9999 fine products: you save the 5–15% tax, and you own the most liquid form of gold on earth. Anything below 99.5% — including all karat jewellery — is taxed normally and trades at a discount to its gold content.
# Investment Grade vs. Jewellery Grade: A Direct Comparison
The takeaway: buy bullion for investment, buy jewellery for enjoyment. Don't confuse the two — jewellery is a terrible investment vehicle because you pay massive retail markups you'll never recover.
# How to Test Gold Purity
If you're buying secondhand gold or want to verify what you own, these are the standard methods Canadian dealers use:
# Visual Inspection and Hallmarks
Start with the stamp. Then examine the piece: discolouration at edges or worn spots revealing different-coloured metal underneath suggests plating, not solid gold.
# Magnet Test (Quick Screening)

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
Gold is not magnetic. If a "gold" bar sticks strongly to a magnet, it's fake. (Note: this only catches crude fakes — sophisticated counterfeits use non-magnetic metals.)
A jeweller files a tiny notch in an inconspicuous spot and applies nitric acid of known strength. Real gold of the marked karat resists the acid; lower-karat gold dissolves. Inexpensive kits exist, but the test damages the piece slightly — leave it to professionals for valuable items.
Devices like the Sigma Metalytics verifier measure electrical conductivity to confirm purity without damaging the item. Most serious Canadian bullion dealers have one and will test in front of you — ask them to.
X-ray fluorescence is the gold standard (pun intended): completely non-destructive and precise to the decimal. Refiners and assay offices use XRF machines. If you're selling a large quantity, paying for an XRF assay ($50–$150) is worthwhile.
# Specific Gravity (Water Displacement)

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
Pure gold is extremely dense (19.32 g/cm³). Weighing an item in air and in water lets you calculate its density — a clever at-home check for bars and coins. Tungsten fakes (tungsten has nearly identical density to gold) can defeat this test, which is why professionals combine methods.
# Frequently Asked Questions
# Is 24K gold better than 22K?
For investment, yes — 24K (.999+) is the standard for bullion, qualifies for the GST/HST exemption, and is the most liquid. For jewellery you wear daily, 22K or 18K is more practical because pure gold is soft and scratches easily. "Better" depends entirely on purpose.
# What does 9999 mean on a Gold Maple Leaf?
It means the coin is 99.99% pure gold — among the purest bullion coins in the world. The Royal Canadian Mint pioneered this standard, and it's a point of national pride in the precious metals industry.
# Is Canadian gold jewellery always marked accurately?
Legitimate Canadian jewellers must comply with the Precious Metals Marking Act, and enforcement is real. Problems arise mainly with secondhand pieces, market-stall sellers, and items bought abroad. When in doubt, have a jeweller test it.
# Does higher karat gold tarnish less?

chunks.title: Gold Purity Explained: 24K vs 22K vs 18K vs 14K
chunks.text:
Yes. Tarnishing comes from the alloy metals (especially copper and silver), not the gold itself. 24K gold essentially never tarnishes; 14K and 10K can develop a patina over years, particularly with exposure to chemicals.
# Can I convert my 14K jewellery into 24K bullion?
Indirectly, yes: sell your jewellery to a dealer or refiner (you'll receive its melt value minus their margin), then use the proceeds to buy bullion. You won't get a 1:1 exchange — expect to lose 10–30% in the conversion due to refining costs and dealer margins.
# Why is some "gold" jewellery so cheap?
Because it isn't solid gold. Gold-plated (GP), gold-filled, and vermeil pieces contain only a thin surface layer of gold. They're costume jewellery, not investments. Always check for solid-gold hallmarks (10K and above) before paying gold prices.

# Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
Here is a number that should make every Canadian gold buyer pause: right now, a 1 oz 2026 Gold Maple Leaf costs C$6,384.09 at TD Bank — and C$6,293.94 at Sprott Money . Same coin, same gold, same country. A gap of roughly C$90 .
That gap is not a rounding error. It is the difference between buying at a bank and buying at a specialist dealer, and it repeats across the market: banks are consistently among the most expensive places to buy gold in Canada, while specialist dealers undercut them on almost every product. This guide compares the two routes — with real numbers — so you can decide where your money goes.
# The head-to-head: what the numbers say
Let's start with the apples-to-apples comparison. On a 1 oz 2026 Gold Maple Leaf, quoted in the same week:
TD Bank: C$6,384.09 — premium of roughly 3.5% over the spot price at the time of the quote
Sprott Money: C$6,293.94 — premium of roughly 2.0% over spot
The Sprott price is about C$90 lower on a single coin. Buy ten ounces and the difference approaches C$900 — real money by any measure.

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
Note that premiums look higher against today's lower spot (around C$5,845/oz in mid-October): relative to current spot, these quotes represent roughly 9% and 8% over. The lesson doesn't change with the spot level — the relative gap between banks and dealers persists in every market, because it comes from the business model, not the price of metal.
TD is not an outlier. Canada's big banks — TD, RBC, Scotiabank, and BMO all sell bullion — price their products with a "trust premium." You are paying for the bank's brand, its vault, and the comfort of buying from an institution you already know. For some buyers that comfort is worth it. For most, it is an expensive habit.
# Why banks charge more
Banks are not really in the bullion business — they are in the banking business. Gold is a side offering, and the pricing reflects that:
Overhead. A bank branch network, compliance apparatus, and vaulting operation are expensive. Those costs land somewhere, and bullion margins are a convenient place.
Limited selection. Banks typically sell a narrow range of standard bars and coins. No competition within their own catalogue means no pressure to sharpen prices.

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
No buyback market-making. Most banks sell gold but do not actively buy it back at competitive rates. Specialist dealers live on the two-way spread — buy and sell — which forces their sell prices closer to spot.
The convenience tax. Walk-in, in-and-out, one familiar institution. Many buyers never compare prices, so banks have little incentive to compete on them.
None of this makes banks dishonest. Bank-sold gold is as authentic as it gets, and for a nervous first-time buyer the reassurance has genuine value. It just isn't the cheapest option, and the premium is measurable.
# The dealer side: who they are and what they charge
Canada has a mature network of specialist bullion dealers, both online and storefront. The established names — the ones with years of track records, published live prices, and active buyback programs — include:
Kitco (Montreal) — one of the world's best-known precious metals brands; deep inventory, excellent price transparency
Silver Gold Bull (Calgary) — fast-growing online dealer with competitive premiums and walk-in service
Border Gold (Vancouver) — long-established, strong in Western Canada

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
Colonial Acres (Kitchener) — respected Ontario dealer with a strong coin business
Sprott Money — competitive pricing on flagship products like the Maple Leaf, as the numbers above show
Dealers compete on the one number that matters: premium over spot . Typical dealer premiums on a 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf run 2–5% over spot for small orders, tightening as order size grows. That is structurally lower than bank pricing for the same coin.
Dealers also tend to offer what banks don't: fractional coins, a wide bar selection, price alerts, storage programs, and — crucially — published buyback prices . A dealer that quotes you a buyback price is showing you the other half of the spread. If they won't buy it back, ask why.
# How to compare prices properly (apples to apples)
Dealer prices move with the spot market, so a fair comparison follows three rules:
Same product. Compare the exact same coin or bar — a 1 oz 2026 Gold Maple Leaf at TD versus the identical coin at Sprott. Different products carry different minting costs and premiums.

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
Same day, same hour. Spot moves by the minute. Screenshot or note the time of each quote, and convert each to "premium over spot" rather than comparing raw dollar figures across different days.
Include all-in costs. A dealer's lower sticker price can be eroded by shipping and insurance; a bank's higher price might include free in-branch pickup. Add shipping, insurance, and any payment-method surcharges (credit cards often add 2–3%) before declaring a winner.
The formula: (quoted price − spot price) ÷ spot price = premium . Whoever has the lower premium on the identical product, all-in, wins.
# The tax angle: GST/HST exemption
One more factor that affects the true cost: investment-grade gold bullion — defined as 99.5% pure or higher — is exempt from GST/HST across Canada. The 1 oz Gold Maple Leaf (99.99% pure) qualifies, as do standard investment bars.
This matters when comparing products, not sellers: a 22K gold coin or jewellery piece may attract GST/HST where a 24K bullion bar doesn't. The exemption applies equally at banks and dealers, so it doesn't change the bank-vs-dealer math — but it does mean you should compare bullion to bullion, and confirm purity before you buy.

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
# Red flags: cheap isn't always better
While banks overcharge, the bargain basement has its own dangers. Walk away from any seller — bank, dealer, or marketplace — that:
Won't quote a price tied to live spot, or can't explain their premium
Pressures you to decide "today only" or demands wire transfer with no paper trail
Sells "gold" without sealed assay packaging or a verifiable mint source
Has no buyback policy and no physical address
Advertises prices dramatically below every established dealer (counterfeit risk)
Stick to dealers with years in business, published prices, and real reviews. Our gold dealers guide walks through the full verification checklist.
On identical products, specialist dealers beat banks on price in Canada — consistently, measurably, and by enough to matter. The C$90 gap between TD and Sprott on a single Maple Leaf is typical, not exceptional. Banks sell certainty and convenience; dealers sell gold at closer to its actual market price.

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
If you value maximum peace of mind and are buying a small amount once, a bank is a defensible choice. If you are building a position over time, the dealer route will save you hundreds — eventually thousands — of dollars. Either way, run the numbers first: check the live gold price , compute the premium over spot, and let the arithmetic decide.
# Frequently asked questions
# Is it safe to buy gold from online dealers in Canada?
Yes, provided you stick to established Canadian dealers with long track records, published live prices, insured shipping, and buyback programs. Avoid ordering from US dealers: customs delays, brokerage fees, and currency conversion can wipe out any savings.
# Why is TD Bank's gold more expensive than Sprott Money's?
Banks price bullion with higher overhead, limited selection, and a convenience premium. Specialist dealers compete directly on premium over spot and make markets in both directions (buy and sell), which keeps their prices tighter to the metal price.
# What is a fair premium over spot for a Gold Maple Leaf in Canada?

chunks.title: Where to Buy Gold in Canada: Banks vs Dealers Compared
chunks.text:
For a 1 oz coin from a reputable dealer, roughly 2–5% over spot is normal for small orders, tightening with volume. Anything dramatically above that deserves a comparison quote; anything dramatically below it deserves suspicion.
# Do I pay GST/HST on gold in Canada?
Not on investment-grade bullion of 99.5% purity or higher — it is exempt nationwide. Lower-purity products and jewellery generally attract GST/HST. The exemption applies at both banks and dealers.
# Can I sell gold back to a bank?
Usually not at competitive rates — most banks are set up to sell, not buy back. Specialist dealers publish buyback prices, which is one reason their business model produces fairer pricing in both directions.
# Should I buy from the Royal Canadian Mint directly?
You can, and the product is beyond reproach. But Mint-direct premiums are often higher than dealer premiums on the same coins — the Mint is a manufacturer, not a discounter. Compare before you commit.

# Understanding gold karats
Karat measures gold purity out of 24 parts: 24K means 24 parts pure gold (99.9%), 22K means 22 parts gold and 2 parts alloy (91.6%), down to 10K at just 41.7% gold. Lower karats are harder, more durable, and cheaper per gram.
Genuine pieces carry a hallmark showing fineness in parts per thousand: 999 for 24K, 916 for 22K, 875 for 21K, 750 for 18K, 585 for 14K and 417 for 10K. This stamp is your most reliable reference when buying from a jeweller or selling \u2014 counterfeit pieces can carry fake stamps, so always buy from reputable dealers.
In Canada, 22K dominates traditional South Asian jewellery, 14K is the everyday high-street standard, and 18K is preferred for diamond settings because the harder alloy grips stones securely. Investment bars and coins, such as Royal Canadian Mint products, are usually 24K (999.9) to track the global spot price as closely as possible.

Karat measures gold purity out of 24 parts: 24K is 99.9% pure gold, 22K is 91.6%, 21K is 87.5%, 18K is 75%, 14K is 58.5% and 10K is 41.7%. The rest is alloy metals that add strength.
# Q 2 . What do hallmark numbers like 916 or 750 mean?
They are the fineness in parts per thousand: 916 means 91.6% gold (22K), 875 means 87.5% (21K), and 750 means 75% (18K). Always check the hallmark before buying or selling.

22K dominates traditional South Asian jewellery for its rich colour and good value; 14K is the everyday standard in Canadian high-street shops; 18K is preferred for diamond settings because the harder alloy holds stones better. 24K is too soft for most jewellery and is used for bars and coins.

Yes — 14K gold contains 58.5% pure gold mixed with alloys. It is durable and affordable, and it is the standard karat for everyday jewellery sold across Canada.

# Gold Calculator Canada
Estimate your gold’s value in Canadian dollars using today’s 24K, 22K, 21K and 18K rates.
# How to use the gold calculator
Enter your gold item\u2019s weight, then pick the unit: grams are the global standard, the tola (11.6638 g) is the traditional South Asian unit widely used by Canada\u2019s South Asian community, and large bars are priced in troy ounces (31.1035 g).
Select the karat stamped on your item. 24K gold is 99.9% pure and used for investment bars and coins such as Royal Canadian Mint products; 22K (91.6%) dominates traditional South Asian jewellery; 18K (75%) is the harder alloy used for diamond-studded designs; and 14K (58.5%) is the standard for everyday Canadian high-street jewellery.
The value is your weight in grams multiplied by today\u2019s per-gram rate for that karat. Note the result is the intrinsic melt value of the raw gold only \u2014 it excludes the making charges a jeweller adds and the sales tax charged on those making charges (5% GST in Alberta and the territories, 12% in BC (5% GST + 7% PST), 13% HST in Ontario, 14.975% GST+QST in Quebec). For the full shop price, use our jewellery cost calculator.

# Jewellery Cost Calculator
Know the full shop price before you buy: gold value + making charges + sales tax.
Note: in Canada, sales tax on jewellery making charges varies by province — Ontario: 13% HST, British Columbia: 12% (5% GST + 7% PST), Alberta: 5% GST, Quebec: 14.975% (GST+QST), other provinces and territories: 5% GST. Select your province above to apply the correct rate. Investment-grade gold (99.5%+ pure, e.g. Royal Canadian Mint bars and Maple Leaf coins) is GST/HST-exempt. Figures are indicative estimates, not a final jeweller quote.
# How jewellery is priced in Canada
Every gold jewellery piece in Canada is priced in three parts. First, the raw gold value: weight in grams multiplied by today\u2019s per-gram rate for the karat \u2014 this part is non-negotiable because it tracks the global market. Second, making charges: the craftsmanship fee, typically CAD 15\u201360 per gram for machine-made pieces and higher for handcrafted luxury designs. Third, sales tax, charged on the making-charges portion: 5% GST in Alberta and the territories, 12% in BC (5% GST + 7% PST), 13% HST in Ontario, 14.975% (GST+QST) in Quebec.

# Zakat on Gold Calculator
Calculate 2.5% zakat on your gold after checking its value against the nisab at today’s rates.
Disclaimer: this calculator is an estimate for guidance only — not a fatwa. Consult a qualified scholar for your situation. The silver nisab is 612.36 g; zakat applies to fully owned gold held for a full lunar year (hawl).
# How zakat on gold is calculated
Zakat on gold becomes due when it reaches the nisab and a full lunar year (hawl) has passed. The nisab is 87.48 grams of pure (24K) gold, valued in Canadian dollars by multiplying by today\u2019s 24K per-gram rate \u2014 so the threshold moves with the market, and the calculator keeps it updated daily.
If your gold\u2019s value meets or exceeds the nisab, zakat is 2.5% of the total value. Lower-karat gold (22K, 18K) is valued at its own per-gram rate, while the nisab comparison uses the pure-gold content \u2014 the calculator handles this using the daily karat rates.

# Q 1 . What is the nisab for gold?
The gold nisab is 87.48 grams of 24K gold (equivalent to 85 grams by some measures). Zakat at 2.5% becomes due when your zakatable gold reaches this threshold and a full lunar year (hawl) has passed.
# Q 2 . Is zakat due on gold jewellery I wear?
Scholars differ: the Hanafi school generally includes worn jewellery in zakatable wealth, while other schools may exempt personal-use jewellery. This calculator shows the numbers; consult a qualified scholar for your situation.

# How buyback pricing works
When you sell used gold, the dealer pays only for the gold content at below the market rate, because they carry melting, refining and resale costs plus their margin. The discount typically runs 3\u20138% off the melt value \u2014 adjust the percentage in the calculator to match the offer you hear in the shop.
Remember that the making charges you paid when buying are never recovered on resale, which is why jewellery is a weaker investment than bars. Before selling, compare at least two or three shops \u2014 in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal or Calgary \u2014 and never accept the first offer you hear.

# Q 1 . Why do dealers pay less than the market gold rate?
Dealers buy below the spot rate to cover melting, refining and resale costs, plus their margin. A 3–8% discount from the melt value is typical — use the adjustable discount to match a shop’s actual offer.
# Q 2 . Do I need my original invoice to sell gold in Canada?
It is not legally required, but carrying the original invoice and keeping the hallmark intact makes the buy-back faster and usually gets you a better price, because the dealer can verify purity instantly.
# Q 3 . Is it better to sell gold jewellery or melt it first?
Dealers pay for the gold content only — making charges and design value are lost on resale. Selling as-is to a reputable jeweller is simplest; melting yourself adds cost and is rarely worthwhile for small quantities.

# Gold Investment Calculator
See how much your gold investment has gained (or lost) versus today’s price.
Note: you enter the past purchase price yourself — we assume no historical prices. The comparison uses today’s indicative 24K rate, excluding making charges and taxes. This is an educational tool, not investment advice.
# How to measure your gold return
Your true return comes from what you actually paid: divide the invested amount by the per-gram price at purchase (from your invoice) to get the grams you own, then multiply by today\u2019s 24K rate. The difference between the two values is your profit or loss in percent.
That is why the calculator asks for your past price instead of assuming generic historical prices \u2014 the shop you bought from, the karat and any premium all shape your personal result. For a conservative estimate, enter your all-in cost including making charges as the past price.

We divide your invested amount by the past per-gram price you enter (from your invoice) to get the grams you bought, then multiply those grams by today’s 24K rate. The difference is your profit or loss. We never assume historical prices — you enter them.
# Q 2 . Are making charges included in the return?
No. The comparison uses the raw 24K gold value on both sides, excluding making charges, sales tax and dealer spreads — which is why jewellery usually shows a lower return than bars. Enter your all-in cost as the past price for a conservative estimate.
